query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles initially formed as homogeneous solid solutions, the retention of structural and chemical stability across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges (473–1923 K) is governed by a thermodynamic balance between configurational entropy and differences in cohesive/surface energies. This balance drives moderate, selective surface segregation—primarily of lower cohesive energy elements such as Cu (and to a lesser extent Pd)—which minimizes the system’s free energy without triggering complete phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals (e.g., Pd, Cu, Pt, Ni, Co) in near-equal atomic ratios forming a homogeneous solid-solution crystal structure.
generation.intervention: Thermal treatment/annealing over the operating temperature range (473–1923 K) under catalytic or thermoelectric conditions.
generation.conditions: Inert or controlled atmosphere to mimic operating catalytic/thermoelectric environments with stepwise temperature increments; measurements conducted in situ or with rapid quenching to capture transient segregation behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation of lower cohesive energy elements (e.g., Cu, Pd) that modulates the nanoparticle’s surface composition without complete bulk phase separation.
generation.mechanism: As temperature increases, the interplay between lowering internal energy (by segregating metals with lower cohesive contributions) and maintaining high configurational entropy drives selective surface enrichment. This process minimizes the Helmholtz free energy (F = U – TS) such that the surface becomes enriched in metals with weaker metallic bonds while the core retains a stable solid-solution structure, preserving overall chemical and structural stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Upon heating, the nanoparticle surfaces will show an increased concentration of Cu (and somewhat Pd) relative to the bulk, while the core remains compositionally uniform. This controlled segregation should coincide with maintained or even enhanced catalytic/thermoelectric performance relative to the room-temperature baseline. Excessive segregation or bulk phase separation, however, would lead to performance degradation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized as homogeneous, equimolar solid solutions at or near room temperature with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds under rapid or moderate thermal ramping in environments that do not accelerate oxidation or excessive diffusion. Under overly prolonged heating or in strongly oxidative conditions, additional phenomena (e.g., bulk phase separation or oxidation) may occur, exceeding the bounds of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative extent of segregation, its kinetics, and the correlation with catalytic or thermoelectric performance are not fully established and may depend on specific compositions and experimental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HEA nanoparticles (e.g., PdCuPtNiCo) with confirmed homogeneous solid-solution structures using a controlled synthesis method. Subject these particles to a series of thermal treatments up to 1923 K under an inert or controlled atmosphere. Employ in situ high-resolution STEM/EDS and X-ray diffraction to monitor surface composition and phase integrity during heating. Concurrently, assess catalytic and thermoelectric performance before, during, and after thermal cycling.
measurements: Surface elemental composition (e.g., via STEM/EDS or atom probe tomography)
XRD patterns to detect any emerging secondary phases or bulk phase separation
Catalytic activity metrics (e.g., ORR rates) or thermoelectric performance parameters
Temperature-dependent structural imaging to monitor morphology changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles do not exhibit any selective surface enrichment (e.g., no increased concentration of low cohesive energy elements relative to the core) and instead show either complete homogeneity or uncontrolled bulk phase separation, or if the catalytic/thermoelectric performance degrades without a corresponding controlled segregation pattern, the hypothesis that balanced selective surface segregation governs their stability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs), characterized as compositionally complex solid solutions with five or more metal elements, have emerged as a novel class of catalytic materials with unique attributes. Because of the remarkable diversity of multielement sites or site ensembles stabilized by configurational entropy, human exploration of the multidimensional design space of HEAs presents a formidable challenge, necessitating an efficient, computational and data-driven strategy over traditional trial-and-error experimentation or physics-based modeling. Leveraging deep learning interatomic potentials for large-scale molecular simulations and pretrained machine learning models of surface reactivity, our approach effectively rationalizes the enhanced activity of a previously synthesized PdCuPtNiCo HEA nanoparticle system for electrochemical oxygen reduction, as corroborated by experimental observations. We contend that this framework deepens our fundamental understanding of the surface reactivity of high-entropy materials and fosters the accelerated development and synthesis of monodisperse HEA nanoparticles as a versatile material platform for catalyzing sustainable chemical and energ

To assess the surface stability of our HEA system under annealing conditions, we employed machine learning interatomic potentials based on graph neural networks, particularly the atomistic line graph neural network (ALIGNN), in molecular simulations to obtain equilibrium configurations. Details of model development can be found in the Method section. Figure 3a presents a parity plot comparing DFT-calculated and ALIGNN-predicted per-atom energies. Both training and test data sets exhibit mean absolute errors (MAEs) below 5 meV/atom, indicating a balanced model without noticeable underfitting or overfitting. To determine the equilibrium surface configurations after high-temperature annealing, canonical Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using the trained deep learning potential, with an equilibrium achieved after approximately 16,000 steps. The occurrence probability of each element across the surface layers, illustrated in Figure 3b, maps the segregation profile perpendicular to the surface. The underlying mechanisms driving Cu and Pd segregation can be elucidated through Helmholtz free energy components F = U – TS of canonical ensembles, encompassing internal energy (U) and entropy (S). According to the cohesion theory, the cohesive energy trend among late transition and noble metals is mainly dictated by the d-band, approximated as where Wd represents the d-band width and Nd is the number of d-electrons. For Cu, with a fully occupied d-band (Nd = 10), its cohesive contribution is minimal, making metallic bonds with Cu energetically less favorable. Consequently, to minimize the system’s internal energy, Cu atoms tend to segregate onto the surface. Pd has only marginally higher cohesive and surface energies compared to Cu, which partially contributes to the surface segregation of Pd. Moreover, given the abundance of Pd in the HEA’s bulk composition (Pd0.25Cu0.20Pt0.20Ni0.22Co0.13 as targeted in our simulations), segregation to the surface occurs as the bulk strives for an equimolar distribution to maximize the configurational entropy, thereby rationalizing the segregation of Pd atoms at the HEA surface as observed in Monte Carlo simulations.
